Compiler Design
SLR Parsing

LR(0) conflicts
The key limitation of LR(0) is:
LR(0) makes reductions without considering the next input symbol.
SLR(1) adds one-symbol lookahead using FOLLOW sets.
LR(0) → no lookahead → more conflicts
SLR(1) → 1−symbol lookahead via FOLLOW → fewer conflicts
                                           Important: SLR(1) does not eliminate every possible conflict; 
2

SLR(1) : Simple LR(1) Parsing
• The key idea is that LR(0) reduces too aggressively, while SLR(1) uses the FOLLOW set to decide when 
a reduction is allowed.
• What is SLR(1)?
• SLR(1) uses the same LR(0) item sets and DFA that we already constructed.
• The difference is in the ACTION table:
• LR(0): If we have 𝐴→𝛽∙, put reduce 𝐴→𝛽for all terminals. 
• SLR(1): Put reduce 𝐴→𝛽only for terminals in FOLLOW(A). 
 
So:           SLR(1) = LR(0) items + FOLLOW sets
3

SLR(1) : Simple LR(1) Parsing
What can the next symbol be when we reduce F → id ?
S’ → T → F → id
S’ → T → T * F → T*id → F*id → id* id
S’→ T → C(T) → C(F) → C(id) 
The top of the stack will be id, and the next input symbol will be either $, *, or )
Follow(F) = { *, ), $ }
When we reduce F → id, the top of the stack will contain: id
And the next input symbol will be one of: $, *, or )
These symbols tell the parser whether it should shift or reduce during 
parsing.
4

SLR(1) : Simple LR(1) Parsing
What can the next symbol be when we reduce C → id ?
S’ → T → C(T) → C(F) → C(id) → id (id) 
Follow(C) = { ( }  
When reducing C → id, the parser checks the FOLLOW(C) set to decide whether a reduction is valid based on 
the upcoming input symbol.
So, the valid lookahead symbol is: '('
5

Is this grammar SLR(1)?
•
In the initial item set (shown in the diagram), both completed items A → ε· and B → ε· appear in the same state.
•
Because Follow(A) = Follow(B) = {a,b}, for lookahead a (or b) both reductions A → ε and B → ε are valid in that same state.
•
That yields a reduce–reduce conflict (two different reductions enabled by the same lookahead), so the SLR(1) decision rules are 
not sufficient — the parsing table would be conflicted.
Conclusion: Grammar is not SLR(1).

IT 302 Compiler Design
Canonical LR Parsing

SLR limitation: lack of context
In SLR parsing, Reduction is allowed 
on all symbols in FOLLOW(R). →→
The problem (lack of context)
•
In context of S → L = R, if lookahead is =, the parser should shift, not reduce.
•
But SLR only looks at FOLLOW sets, not the specific item context.
•
Since = is in FOLLOW(R), SLR wrongly allows reduction, creating a shift/reduce conflict.
30

Why LR(1) solves it
• In LR(1), items carry lookahead symbols. LR (1) = LR (0) Item + Lookahead Symbols
• So instead of just R → L •, we’d have:
• R → L •, $ (reduce only on $)
• R → L •, = would not exist in this state, because in the context of S → L = R, reduction on = is 
invalid.
• This disambiguates the decision:
• On =, shift.
• On $, reduce.
•
Note:
•
SLR limitation: it uses FOLLOW sets without context, so reductions may be applied in situations where they are 
not valid, leading to false conflicts.
•
LR(1) overcomes this by attaching the precise lookahead to each item, preserving context.
SLR(1)→FOLLOW-based, less context​ 
LR(1) →Item−specific lookahead, more context
Thus, LR(1) preserves the context of each LR item and can 
eliminate conflicts that SLR(1) cannot.
31

Solution: Canonical LR(1)
• Extend the definition of configuration 
• Remember lookahead 
• New closure method 
• Extend the definition of Successor
32

Extend the definition of configuration 
• In LR(0)/SLR, a configuration (item) looks like: [A → α • β]
• In LR(1), we extend it to: [A → α • β, a]
• where a is a lookahead terminal that is expected to follow A.
• So, each item carries both the parsing progress (•) and a lookahead context.
where:
•
A → αβ is a production.
•
• marks the current parsing position in the right-hand side.
•
a ∈ T ∪ {$} is the lookahead symbol → the terminal that is expected to follow A.
So, it encodes both progress in parsing and what we expect next.

• Validity of a Configuration
•
Start from the augmented start symbol S’.
•
There exists a rightmost derivation where:
1.
S ⇒* δ A h (we are about to expand A).
2.
Then A ⇒ α β, so S ⇒* δ α β ⴄ.
3.
The lookahead condition:
•
If ⴄ = aγ → the first symbol of the suffix is a.
•
If ⴄ = ε (we’re at the end), then a = $.
34

Points to be Noted
• LR(1) item = production + dot position + lookahead symbol.
• An item [A → α • β, a] is valid if it matches a rightmost derivation where a is the 
actual next terminal (or $ at the end).
• Multiple lookaheads can be grouped as [A → α • β, a/b/c].
• This precise context handling is why LR(1) parsers are more powerful than SLR(1).
35

LR(1) Closure: The new Closure Method
• Closure property: If [A → a•B, a] is in set, then [B →• γ, b] is in set if b € First(a) 
1st : [A→α•Bβ,a] means: we are in the middle of parsing B in production A → αBβ, with lookahead a.
2nd: What does Closure mean? If you expect a B next, you must also consider all ways of deriving B.
 
 
So for every production B→γ, add:   [B→•γ, b]
This is the key LR(1) difference from SLR:
•
Lookahead set = First(β a), where
•
β is what follows B in the original item,
•
a is the original lookahead.
